meta.dek: Every Fernhill order, from the first click to the parcel on the porch, used to pass through one system built in {{project.monolith_year}}. meta.description: An illustrated status report on Keystone, the move of Fernhill Outfitters' order platform from one monolith to five services.

Built by the chronicle plugin from two files: a facts file gathered from the sources above, and a story file that arranges them. Every figure on the page comes from the facts file, and computed figures come from code; hover or tap a figure to see its source. The illustrations were drawn as SVG for this page and painted in ink and watercolor by a short OpenCV program: no stock art, no image model.

blocks.text:
Fernhill's order management system went live in {{project.monolith_year}}. By early 2025 it held {{project.monolith_loc|compact}} lines of Java in a single repository and shipped {{delivery.deploys_then|plain}} releases a week, each release a weekend of work. A change took a median {{delivery.lead_then}} to reach customers, and {{delivery.cfr_then}} of releases needed a fix or a rollback.

The cost showed up at the checkout. Its 95th-percentile response time was {{experience.p95_then}}.

blocks.caption: The monolith, drawn as what it behaved like: one cabinet with a drawer for every part of the order, chained so that nothing moves unless everything moves.

spots.label: One codebase
spots.title: {{project.monolith_loc|compact}} lines in one repository
spots.text: Catalog, cart, checkout, payments and fulfillment shared one deploy, one database and one release train.

spots.label: One release
spots.title: {{delivery.deploys_then|plain}} releases a week
spots.text: Every change waited for the whole cabinet: a median {{delivery.lead_then}} from first commit to customers, with {{delivery.cfr_then}} of releases needing a fix or a rollback.

spots.label: The night call
spots.title: {{delivery.mttr_then}} to restore
spots.text: A bad release often meant restoring from backup. Median time to restore in March 2025 was {{delivery.mttr_then}}.

blocks.text: Keystone's plan was the **strangler pattern**: build new services beside the old system, move one capability at a time, and keep the monolith running as the fallback until the last one has moved. In the cabinet's terms, empty one drawer at a time, and never pull the cabinet out while orders are still filed in it.

chapters.title: Tools on the wall before the first parcel
chapters.dek: The first phase moved no traffic at all. It built what every later service starts from.

blocks.text:
Nothing a customer could see shipped in the first phase. The team built a paved road instead, a shared tool set every squad takes from one wall: one pipeline template, shared clusters, an event bus and tracing that follows an order across services. Every service since has started from that template.

The payoff shows in the four delivery measures the industry tracks. Deploys went from {{delivery.deploys_then}} to {{delivery.deploys_now}}, about {{delivery.deploy_ratio}} as many. Lead time fell from {{delivery.lead_then}} to {{delivery.lead_now}}. The share of changes that fail fell from {{delivery.cfr_then}} to {{delivery.cfr_now}}, and time to restore from {{delivery.mttr_then}} to {{delivery.mttr_now}}.

blocks.title: The lesson

blocks.text: A Fernhill order takes six steps from the first click to the porch. {{project.services_live|plain}} of them now run entirely on Keystone, one is moving now, and the last two move with fulfillment.

steps.text: **July 2025.** The catalog read API goes first, in shadow mode, answering requests the monolith also answers so the two can be compared. Product pages are the largest slice of traffic, so the share jumps once reads switch over.
**October 2025.** Carts move. For the first time Keystone holds customer state as well as reads.

**November to February.** The share creeps from {{migration.share.4}}% to {{migration.share.7}}%. Black Friday exposed a retry storm between the two systems, and the team spent {{reliability.reset_months}} on reliability before moving another service.
**March 2026.** Checkout moves and the share passes half.
**Since June.** Payments run on both platforms, {{migration.payments_dual_run}} of authorizations on the new one. The cutover on {{migration.payments_cutover|date}} moves the fourth service.

chapters.title: The morning the belt jammed
chapters.dek: Black Friday 2025, a little before ten.

blocks.text:
{{reliability.weeks_after_cart}} after carts moved, Black Friday morning exposed a fault between the two systems. A slow response from the monolith's inventory sync triggered retries, the retries multiplied, and the flood of events backed up into the cart service until its database had no connections left.

Cart API errors peaked at {{reliability.incident_peak_err}}. Customers felt it for {{reliability.incident_minutes}}, and analytics estimates {{reliability.incident_carts}} carts were abandoned in that window.

blocks.caption: Black Friday 2025 as a jammed conveyor: cart events piled up faster than the cart service could clear them.

spots.label: The pool runs dry
spots.title: {{reliability.pool_exhausted_at}}
spots.text: All {{reliability.incident_pool}} cart database connections were in use. Requests queued, then failed.

spots.label: Abandoned carts
spots.title: {{reliability.incident_carts}} carts
spots.text: Analytics estimates that many carts were abandoned in the {{reliability.incident_minutes}} of customer impact.

spots.label: The fallback
spots.title: Carts go back to the monolith
spots.text: The incident commander pulled the one lever the migration plan had kept for this: cart traffic back to the old path.

blocks.title: How one slow sync jammed the cart
blocks.subtitle: Hover or tap a box for the detail, or step through the chain.
blocks.alt: Diagram: the monolith's inventory sync retries flood cart events, the cart service falls behind, its database pool fills, and shoppers see errors; a fallback switch sends carts back to the monolith's cart path.

steps.title: The flood
steps.text: A slow inventory sync retried with no backoff, and cart events rose to {{reliability.incident_multiple}} a normal Friday.

steps.title: The bottleneck
steps.text: The cart service fell behind by {{reliability.incident_lag|compact}} messages and used every one of its {{reliability.incident_pool}} database connections.

steps.title: The failure
steps.text: Requests queued, then failed: {{reliability.incident_peak_err}} of cart calls at the peak.

steps.title: The fallback
steps.text: The fallback switch sent carts back to the monolith, which the plan had kept running for exactly this.

blocks.title: {{reliability.incident_minutes}}, step by step
blocks.subtitle: Cart API error rate, Eastern time. Step through the response.

steps.title: The retries start
steps.text: The monolith's inventory sync times out and retries without backoff. Events on the cart topic rise to {{reliability.incident_multiple}} their normal rate.

steps.title: The queue backs up
steps.text: Consumer lag on cart events passes {{reliability.incident_lag|compact}} messages.

steps.title: The pool runs dry
steps.text: All {{reliability.incident_pool}} database connections in the cart service are in use. Requests queue, then fail.

steps.title: The page fires
steps.text: The reliability alert pages the on-call engineer, who acknowledges it and opens an incident.

steps.title: Walk the traffic back
steps.text: The incident commander routes cart traffic back to the monolith, which the strangler design kept running for exactly this. Errors start to fall.

steps.title: Stop the flood
steps.text: The inventory sync is paused at the source and the lag drains.

steps.title: Recovered
steps.text: Errors are back to their normal level. The postmortem produced {{reliability.incident_actions}} actions; the last closed on {{reliability.actions_closed|date}}.

blocks.text: We didn't fix the new path that morning. We sent the carts back down the old one, and then we fixed it.
blocks.role: incident commander, Cart and Checkout lead

blocks.text: Keep the old path running until the new one has survived a peak. The fallback ended the outage in {{reliability.incident_minutes}}, and this year's load test ran at {{reliability.loadtest_multiple}} last year's peak.

blocks.title: What could still go wrong
blocks.subtitle: Open risks by likelihood and impact. Select one for the mitigation.

items.title: Payments cutover lands just before peak season
items.text: The cutover on {{migration.payments_cutover|date}} is {{migration.cutover_to_freeze_days}} before the peak-season freeze. Mitigation: the monolith payment path stays on standby through {{migration.standby_end|date}}, so payments can move back.

items.title: Monolith license renews if switch-off slips
items.text: Missing the {{migration.decommission_target|month}} switch-off triggers a {{migration.license_renewal}} renewal on {{migration.renewal_date|date}}. Mitigation: negotiate a short extension option now.

items.title: Scope keeps growing
items.text: Scope has grown {{plan.scope_growth_pct}} since kickoff, {{plan.growth_recent}} a sprint over the last {{plan.window}}. Mitigation: freeze fulfillment scope at the current epics.

items.title: Two people hold the ledger knowledge
items.text: Reconciliation logic lives in two engineers' heads. Mitigation: a pairing rotation and written runbooks, both under way.

items.title: Logistics partner API limits
items.text: The logistics partner caps requests per minute below our projected peak. Mitigation: batching and a queue in the adapter.

items.title: Peak-season capacity
items.text: Load tested at {{reliability.loadtest_multiple}} last year's peak in September. Watch item only.

chapters.title: A faster checkout, then a cheaper one
chapters.caption: The checkout counter: the stopwatch shows the new 95th-percentile checkout time; the bills are why the savings wait for switch-off.

blocks.text: The clearest result is at the checkout. Its 95th-percentile response time was {{experience.p95_then}} when the project began and is {{experience.p95_now}} now; most of that drop came in March and April, as checkout moved. Conversion rose over the following months, from {{experience.conversion_then}} in February to {{experience.conversion_now}} in September, a gain of {{experience.conversion_gain|plain}} percentage points.

blocks.title: Checkout latency fell in the two months after checkout moved
blocks.subtitle: 95th percentile response time, milliseconds, monthly

blocks.text: The bill has not followed yet. For as long as both systems run, Fernhill pays for both: {{cost.dual_run}} a month in cloud spend on top of the data center. Most of the savings, {{cost.monthly_saving}} a month, arrives only when the monolith is switched off, so every month of delay has a price.

blocks.title: When does the last step move?
blocks.subtitle: Drag the pace and the scope growth. The projection updates the finish date.
blocks.text: A straight-line projection from the last {{plan.window}}. It ignores holidays and the peak-season freeze, so treat the date as the earliest likely.

**Three decisions for this review.** First, confirm the payments cutover on {{migration.payments_cutover|date}}, with the monolith payment path on standby through {{migration.standby_end|date}}. Second, freeze fulfillment scope at its current epics: at the recent pace and scope growth fulfillment lands on {{plan.forecast_finish|date}}, {{plan.forecast_weeks_late}} after the March target, and with scope frozen the same pace lands it on {{plan.forecast_finish_frozen|date}}. Third, negotiate a license extension option now, so a short slip past {{migration.decommission_target|month}} does not force a full {{migration.license_renewal}} renewal.
